extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, and scientists learning principles of experimental inquiry and causal inference
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and canonical canons for discovering causal relations by observation and experiment, including the Method of Difference, Method of Agreement, their joint/indirect use, the Method of Residues, and the Method of Concomitant Variations. Focuses on requirements, examples, limitations, and precautions for each method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine causation by comparing two instances that agree in all circumstances except the presence or absence of a single antecedent (A B C vs B C), so that the difference in consequent (a vs absence of a) can be ascribed to that antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires artificially produced experiments or rapid introduction of a single definite change so that pre-existing circumstances can be assumed identical except for the one introduced change. Examples: bringing an object into a familiar state, plunging a bird into carbonic acid gas (with repetition). Caveats: spontaneous natural instances rarely satisfy these requisitions because of complexity and multiplicity of coexisting circumstances; must watch for the possibility that the observed effect was produced not by the change itself but by the means used to effect the change (testable by further experiments). To establish causation by this method one needs the positive and the negative instance required by the canon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: If every instance in which a phenomenon occurs shares a particular antecedent, that antecedent is connected with the phenomenon (an invariable antecedent or consequent is identified by agreement among instances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicable to any observed instances (including cases where artificial experimentation is impossible). Leads to 'laws of phenomena' or uniformities but does not by itself establish cause vs effect. To determine causal direction, one must be able to produce the effect by introducing the antecedent (i.e., apply the Method of Difference). Often used to suggest candidate antecedents to test by the Method of Difference or as a fallback when Difference is impracticable. Not definitive if other unobserved constant antecedents exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference (Indirect Method of Difference) / THIRD CANON
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more instances in which the phenomenon occurs have only one circumstance in common, while two or more instances in which it does not occur have nothing in common save the absence of that circumstance, then that circumstance is the effect, or the cause, or an indispensable part of the cause, of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructed by a double employment of the Method of Agreement: show (a) all positive instances share A, and (b) all negative instances lack A. This gives positive and negative instances that together resemble the Method of Difference. It extends the Method of Agreement but is not equivalent to a direct Method of Difference because it cannot guarantee that the affirmative instances agree in no other antecedent or that the negative instances agree in nothing but the negation of A. Use when direct isolation is impossible. Still subject to uncertainty from unobserved common factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues / FOURTH CANON
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtract from a complex phenomenon the portions which, by previous inductions, can be assigned to known causes; the remainder (residue) is the effect of the remaining antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essentially a form of Method of Difference: if effects of some antecedents (A and B) are known, subtract their effects from A B C → a b c to infer that residual c is due to C. Valid and rigorous only if the previous inductions (identifying effects of A and B) are themselves reliable (preferably derived by infallible methods) and if we are certain C is the only remaining antecedent for the residue. Otherwise, the conclusion is provisional and should be confirmed by producing C separately or by deductive account from known laws. Very useful for discovering obscure causes and effects that are masked by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations / FIFTH CANON
rubrics_metrics.description: When one phenomenon varies in any manner whenever another phenomenon varies in some particular manner, the former is either a cause or an effect of that phenomenon, or is connected through some causal relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used especially when antecedents cannot be wholly excluded (permanent causes). If modifications in A are invariably followed by corresponding modifications in a, infer a causal connection (though direction may be ambiguous—both may be effects of a common cause). To establish directionality attempt to produce one set of variations by means of the other. Precautions: retain other antecedents unchanged while varying the candidate cause (use Method of Difference to corroborate concomitance); knowledge of absolute quantities of A and a improves inference; beware of extrapolating numerical laws beyond observed limits and of hidden counteracting causes or changes in agent properties; small observed variation ranges can make different numerical laws indistinguishable in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental-control requirements and limitations common to the methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles for applying the methods reliably: ensure pre-existing state of circumstances is well known; introduce changes rapidly/definitely; retain other antecedents unchanged when varying one; seek both positive and negative instances where possible; be cautious about inferring causation from agreement or concomitance without being able to isolate or reproduce the antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights practicalities: artificial experiments are often necessary for Difference; spontaneous natural cases seldom provide perfect pairs; when isolation is impossible, use Agreement or Concomitant Variations and then seek corroboration; check that effects are not due to the means of producing changes; when total exclusion of a cause is impossible, seek modifications (quantity or positional changes) and observe corresponding changes in effect. Always consider possible unobserved antecedents or common causes; verify prior inductions used in Residues; avoid overreliance on narrow variation ranges for numerical extrapolation.
